title: 'A challenge, not a checklist'
subtitle: 'One map a week in 2027. The topic stays open.'

## Follow the question

This project takes inspiration from the [30DayMapChallenge galleries](https://30daymapchallenge.com/galleries/) and [Esri’s 2025 collection](https://storyscape-esriwhere.hub.arcgis.com/pages/2025-30-day-map-challenge). Instead of following a fixed sequence of prompts, I choose a subject that interests me each week.

Variety matters: different scales, sources, techniques, visual styles, and levels of effort. Some weeks may be substantial analyses; others may be a quick experiment.

## Tag after making

Each published map can have three kinds of metadata:

| Dimension | Examples | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Subject | Iceland, games, environment | What is being explored |
| Technique | Points, flow map, raster | How the story is drawn |
| Historical prompt | Exact year, day, and prompt | A verified link to an earlier challenge |

Exact historical matches are recorded separately from loose thematic connections. The historical prompt archive below gives us a reference for those tags; coverage by my own maps will grow as the atlas develops.

## What keeps coming back?

Across the **240 daily prompts announced for 2019–2026**, a few foundations return again and again. **Points, Lines, and Polygons** open every edition. **Hexagons and Raster** also appear in all eight years, although their positions change. These five themes form a remarkably consistent backbone to the challenge.

The recurring prompts also make room for changing how a map is made. **Analog mapping** and **OpenStreetMap** each feature in six editions; **3D** and **trying a new tool** appear in five. Alongside subjects such as population, water, and boundaries, these prompts make experimentation part of the challenge itself.

`NULL` is the actual prompt title, used for missing data or absence; it is not an empty database value. These counts measure **announced prompts**, not the number or popularity of maps submitted.

### How the themes are grouped

The [official annual lists](https://30daymapchallenge.com/2019/) contain **158 distinct titles**. For this atlas, I have grouped wording variants into **133 themes** and assigned each a primary category. For example, “Map with a new tool” and “New tool” count together, as do OpenStreetMap prompts with different “Data challenge” prefixes. Analog and pen-and-paper prompts are grouped as analog mapping.

These groupings and the eight broad categories are **editorial choices, not official challenge labels**. Related prompts are not automatically treated as identical: five-minute and ten-minute maps remain separate, as do monochrome and black-and-white maps. There are **40 grouped themes recurring across years**, compared with **32 recurring exact titles**. The original wording and the reason for each grouping remain available in the database.

::: {.callout-note}
### A dated snapshot

This analysis was prepared on **14 November 2026**. The 2026 edition is still underway, and its full announced schedule is included—even prompts whose dates have not yet arrived. The database also provides a view restricted to the completed 2019–2025 editions.
:::

### Explore the data

Download the [SQLite database](data/challenge/30daymapchallenge.sqlite), the [complete theme ranking (CSV)](data/challenge/theme_frequency.csv), or the [original prompts with categories and source links (CSV)](data/challenge/prompt_details.csv). The [data notes and example queries](https://github.com/tungufoss/maps/tree/main/data/challenge) explain the classification and how to reproduce the counts from the pinned [official source tables](https://github.com/tjukanovt/30DayMapChallenge/tree/aaf2e251d929cc61cc8d5620a4b749f304f5b67a/includes).

For my weekly project, this is a way to notice patterns and seek variety. A recurring theme can be a useful starting point; it does not have to become the next assignment.

## A sustainable weekly rhythm

1. Choose a question and assess the data.
2. Prepare, analyse, and map it.
3. Write the finding, limitations, and method.
4. Export the LinkedIn image and prepare the post.
5. Publish the page and record its tags.

The idea bank remains editable. It is a source of possibilities, not a predetermined timetable.
